extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; anyone learning or teaching mathematical problem-solving heuristics
extracted.subtask_description: Heuristics and teaching guidelines for solving mathematical problems: understanding the problem, devising a plan, carrying out the plan, and reflecting on the solution. Intended for classroom use (teachers) and self-study (students/problem-solvers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four phases of problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Try repeatedly to change your point of view through four phases: (1) Understanding the problem, (2) Devising a plan, (3) Carrying out the plan, (4) Looking back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each phase is important; do not omit any. Jumping immediately to computations without understanding or planning is frequently counterproductive. The list of questions/suggestions in the book is organized according to these four phases and is to be used in that order when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition? Is it possible to satisfy the condition? Is the condition sufficient to determine the unknown? Or is it insufficient, redundant, or contradictory?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbal statement must be understood; the student should be able to state the problem fluently and point out the unknown, data, and condition. Clarify the aim and ensure the problem is reasonable and interesting for the learner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw a figure and introduce suitable notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw a figure if one is connected with the problem and introduce suitable notation for the objects involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out on the figure the unknown and the data; choose appropriate symbols and think about the objects for which signs are chosen. Visual representation often clarifies relations and suggests approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate the various parts of the condition; write them down
rubrics_metrics.description: Split the condition into appropriate parts and write them down explicitly (e.g., distinguish phases, separate constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking a condition into parts can reveal subproblems or phases of motion/process; it helps set up equations or identify independent pieces to tackle. Many worked examples in the book illustrate this (e.g., splitting movement into phases or decomposing algebraic conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the connection between the data and the unknown (devise a plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for the connection that links the data to the unknown; if an immediate connection cannot be found, consider auxiliary problems to obtain a plan of solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceiving the idea of a plan is often the main achievement. Questions and suggestions are intended to provoke such ideas; the 'bright idea' may arrive gradually or suddenly. The plan outlines which computations/constructions to perform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use related problems, theorems, and known methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: Have you seen it before? Do you know a related problem or a theorem that could be useful? Could you use a result or method from a solved related problem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to think of familiar problems with the same or similar unknown; reusing known results/methods or introducing auxiliary elements to make them applicable is recommended. Go back to definitions to restate the problem if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restate, generalize, specialize, or consider analogous problems
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot solve the problem as stated, try more accessible related problems: make it more general or more special, look for analogous problems, or attempt to solve a part of the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping only part of the condition, dropping others, or changing unknown/data may produce a problem nearer to something solvable. Constructing and solving a simplified or related problem can guide toward the original solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Did you use all the data? (diagnosis of omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether you have used all the given data and the whole condition; ensure essential notions involved in the problem are taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to use available data is a common error. Reexamine the statement: some parts may be redundant or contradictory, but confirm that necessary pieces have been applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce auxiliary elements / auxiliary problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce helpful auxiliary elements or consider auxiliary problems when a direct connection between data and unknown is not apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auxiliary constructions, added variables, or intermediate problems can make known methods applicable. The dictionary entries and examples show many standard auxiliary moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary estimate and plausibility checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Make preliminary estimates of the unknown or test plausibility (e.g., rough bounds, order-of-magnitude checks, test by dimension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary estimates can be useful or necessary (example: estimating number of pages to determine digits needed). Use plausibility checks to guide approach and detect impossibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction and pattern observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe patterns and consider discovery by induction; formulate a conjectured general law and check it (prove by induction if appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery by induction needs observation of examples, their initial and final terms, and verification of the inductive step. Many enumeration and sequence problems in the book illustrate this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrying out the plan: check each step
rubrics_metrics.description: While executing your plan, check each step: can you see clearly that the step is correct? Can you prove that it is correct?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mechanical execution without verification. Checking intermediate steps reduces mistakes and ensures the plan is valid; correctness of each step should be demonstrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Looking back: review and reflect
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the completed solution: Can you check the result? Can you check the argument? Can you derive the result differently? Can you see it at a glance? Can you use the result or method for some other problem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection consolidates learning, may yield simpler/insightful arguments, and helps generalize methods to other problems. The book emphasizes deriving alternative solutions and applying results elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher's balance of help (not too much, not too little)
rubrics_metrics.description: When helping students, give assistance that leaves them a reasonable share of the work: not too much and not too little; help discreetly and unobtrusively so students retain an illusion of independent work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put yourself in the student's place to see what would occur to them; ask questions or indicate steps that could have occurred to the student. Help should develop students' abilities to solve future problems independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use questions and suggestions to provoke mental operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ carefully chosen questions and suggestions (e.g., 'What is the unknown?', 'Look at the unknown!') to provoke the mental operations that lead to solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The collected list of questions/suggestions enumerates mental operations typically useful in problem solving; asking them repeatedly helps students internalize them and apply them automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality and common-sense heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer general, natural, simple, common-sense questions and suggestions that are widely applicable across problem types and subject matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heuristics are designed to be general-purpose (applicable to algebraic, geometric, theoretical, practical problems, etc.). Their generality makes them unobtrusive and often effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and practice to acquire skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop problem-solving skill through imitation (observing how others solve problems) and extensive practice (doing many problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching should instill interest and provide plentiful opportunities for imitation and practice; repeated exposure to the key questions will help students internalize mental operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate by decomposing, recombining, and using symmetry/special structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use decomposition and recombination, exploit symmetry and special structure of the problem to simplify and discover relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many dictionary entries and examples (e.g., splitting conditions, using symmetry of figures or algebraic expressions) illustrate these techniques as standard heuristic moves.
